pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–14 years

- **Topic:** The Reactivity Series

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry, Chemical reactions):** pupils are taught "the use of the reactivity series to predict the outcome of displacement reactions" and the reactions of metals with acids, and are expected to represent reactions by word equations; the reactivity series and reduction of metal oxides with carbon underpin metal extraction.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-2):** analyse and interpret data on the properties of reactants and products to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred — displacement is evidenced by colour change, temperature change and a deposited metal.

- **Operational details:** Establish the ordered list of common metals (potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold) as a ranking of how strongly each metal holds on to — or grabs — electrons/oxygen. Ground the order in observed evidence: vigour of reaction with water and with acid. Then teach the two big payoffs: (1) displacement — a more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of its compound (e.g. iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper, with the tell-tale orange copper coating); (2) extraction — carbon sits partway up the series, so it can reduce oxides of metals BELOW it (iron) but not those ABOVE it (aluminium, which needs electrolysis). Tie the order to history: gold found native, iron smelted with carbon since antiquity, aluminium only isolated once electricity was available.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early to formal). Given two metals or a metal and a metal-salt solution, the child predicts whether displacement happens and explains, using position in the series, why carbon extracts iron but not aluminium.
bestPractices: Build the series from evidence — have pupils rank metals by observed vigour with water and acid — rather than issuing the order as a mnemonic to memorise.
Teach displacement as the operational meaning of 'more reactive': a metal higher in the series pushes a lower one out of its compound, seen as a deposited metal and a colour change.
Use the position of carbon in the series to explain the industrial dividing line — carbon reduces oxides below it (iron) but metals above it (aluminium) need electrolysis.
Connect the series to the historical timeline of metal use (gold native, iron smelted, aluminium electrolytic) so the abstract order carries a concrete story.
Keep representation at word-equation level and reason qualitatively; save electrode half-equations and quantitative electrolysis for KS4.
keyRepresentations: The vertical reactivity ladder from potassium (top) to gold (bottom), with carbon and hydrogen marked as reference points.
A displacement grid (metal strips × metal-salt solutions) showing which pairings react.
Word equations for displacement, e.g. iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper.
A reaction-vigour bar chart from metal + water/acid tests.
A historical timeline linking extraction difficulty to when each metal came into use.
commonMisconceptions: Treating the series as an arbitrary list to memorise rather than an ordering by measurable reactivity.
Thinking any metal can displace any other, rather than only a more reactive metal displacing a less reactive one.
Believing carbon can extract all metals, missing that metals above carbon (e.g. aluminium) need electrolysis.
Confusing 'reactive' with 'strong' or 'heavy' — assuming gold or iron must be very reactive because they are hard or dense.
Assuming the deposited copper in a displacement reaction is a coating of the original metal rather than newly formed copper metal.

learn.summary: Learners build the reactivity series of common metals (potassium down to gold) from observed evidence rather than memorising a mnemonic, then use positions in the series to predict displacement reactions and to explain why carbon can extract some metals (iron) but not others (aluminium, which needs electrolysis). Representation stays at the word-equation, qualitative level appropriate for ages 12–14; electrode half-equations and quantitative electrolysis are deferred to later study.

activities.title: Rank the metals by observed vigour
feedback: If a learner places a metal by its hardness, weight, or value, point them back to the recorded reaction evidence: soft, light sodium reacts far more vigorously than dense, heavy, valuable gold. Ranking follows how eagerly it reacts, not how strong or heavy it is.
If the order is handed back as a memorised string with no justification, ask them to point to the specific observation (fizz rate, temperature change) that supports one pair's ordering.
Confirm correct placements by connecting them to the observation: 'Yes — copper did nothing with acid, so it sits low.'
activities.rationale: Deriving the series from comparative observation targets the core misconception that the list is arbitrary and anchors 'reactive' in observable behaviour rather than physical properties. Building order from evidence matches the KS3 expectation to use the reactivity series and study reactions of metals with acids, and the NGSS emphasis on interpreting data to determine whether a reaction occurred. The most vigorous metals are kept to simulation/demonstration on safety grounds.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use the reactivity series to predict the outcome of displacement reactions and study reactions of metals with acids.
Analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-2] they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred.
learnerActions: Observe each of several metals reacting with water and, separately, with dilute acid, recording what happens: fizzing rate, bubbles, any temperature rise, whether anything happens at all. The most reactive metals (potassium, sodium) are never handled by learners: their reactions with water are shown by simulation or teacher demonstration only, and their reactions with acid are far too violent to demonstrate, so these are shown by simulation only. Safer metals (e.g. magnesium, zinc, iron, copper) can be tested hands-on where feasible.

Use the observations to arrange the metals into an ordered list from most reactive to least reactive. For example, note from the demonstration/simulation that potassium reacts violently, that magnesium fizzes strongly in acid, and that copper shows essentially no reaction.
Mark where carbon and hydrogen sit as reference points once the metal order is established from the evidence.
Write a short justification for the placement of two chosen metals, citing the specific observation (e.g. 'magnesium is above zinc because it fizzed faster in the same acid').
activities.intendedInsight: The reactivity series is an ordering by measurable reactivity — how vigorously a metal reacts with water and acid — not an arbitrary list to recite. Position reflects evidence.

activities.title: Displacement grid — more reactive pushes out less reactive
feedback: If a learner predicts that any two metals/solution pairings react, show the empty cells: copper in magnesium sulfate does nothing. Displacement runs one direction only — more reactive displaces less reactive.
If a learner says the orange solid is a coating of the iron, clarify that iron has dissolved into solution (forming iron sulfate) while copper has come out of solution as new copper metal.
Reinforce correct predictions by tying them to series position: 'Magnesium is above copper, so it displaces it — exactly what you saw.'
activities.rationale: A comparison grid makes the directionality of displacement visible and directly confronts the 'any two metals react' and 'coating is the original metal' misconceptions. Word equations keep representation at the appropriate KS3 level. Running comparative reactions and interpreting the outcomes matches both the UK displacement standard and the NGSS data-interpretation emphasis.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use the reactivity series to predict the outcome of displacement reactions and study reactions of metals with acids.
Analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-2] they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred.
learnerActions: Lower each metal strip (e.g. iron nail, zinc, magnesium, copper) into each of several metal-salt solutions (e.g. copper sulfate, magnesium sulfate, zinc sulfate) and record which pairings react and which do nothing.
Observe the tell-tale signs of displacement: an iron nail in blue copper sulfate grows an orange copper coating while the blue colour fades.
For each cell of the grid, state before testing whether you expect a reaction based on the series, then compare with what happens.
Write the word equation for a reaction that occurred, e.g. iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper.
Explain whether the orange solid on the nail is the original metal or newly formed copper.
activities.intendedInsight: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its compound, and the reaction runs only one way. The deposited metal (e.g. copper) is newly formed, not a transferred coating of the original metal.

activities.title: Extraction bench — why carbon works for iron but not aluminium
feedback: If a learner thinks carbon can extract all metals, revisit carbon's position: metals above it (aluminium) resist reduction by carbon and need electrolysis.

If a learner says gold is unreactive because it is rare or precious, flip the causation: gold is found native and never tarnishes because it is unreactive; iron and aluminium are harder to extract because they are more reactive.
Confirm sound reasoning that connects position → extraction method → historical order.
activities.rationale: Using carbon's position to explain the industrial dividing line is a direct KS3/RSC objective and targets the misconception that carbon extracts all metals and the reversed cause–effect about gold's rarity. The historical strand gives the abstract order a concrete narrative. RSC resources state carbon's extraction limit as a chemistry principle; the activity presents it qualitatively.
sourceClaims: Carbon can reduce the oxides of metals less reactive than itself (e.g. iron) but not more reactive metals (e.g. aluminium), which require electrolysis.
learnerActions: Watch a teacher demonstration or simulation of heating a metal oxide with carbon and record the result: iron oxide is reduced to iron, while aluminium oxide is not reduced. (This is a high-temperature reaction, so it is demonstrated or simulated, not run hands-on by learners.)
Locate carbon's position in the series and identify which metal oxides lie below it (can be reduced by carbon) and which lie above it (cannot).
State the method needed to extract aluminium (electrolysis) and explain why carbon alone is not enough.

Build a short timeline linking extraction difficulty to history: gold found native (unreactive), iron smelted with carbon since antiquity, aluminium first isolated only in the 1820s (using an even more reactive metal, not carbon) and made cheaply in bulk only after industrial electrolysis began in the 1880s.
Explain the direction of cause and effect: gold is found as pure nuggets because it is unreactive — its rarity does not cause its low reactivity.
activities.intendedInsight: Carbon can reduce oxides of metals below it in the series (e.g. iron) but not those above it (e.g. aluminium), which require electrolysis. Reactivity causes the extraction difficulty and the historical timeline, not the other way round.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: the paired beakers
feedback: 'Copper wins because it is tougher/stronger' → separate chemical reactivity from physical strength: magnesium is more reactive than copper regardless of hardness, so magnesium displaces copper.
'Both react' → displacement runs one way only; copper is below magnesium, so copper cannot displace magnesium.
Full credit depends on predicting the single correct reaction and giving the direction before observing, using series position — not on which metal looks stronger or heavier.
For the chained case: magnesium is above zinc, which is above iron, so magnesium displaces iron from iron sulfate — high confidence from the transitive ordering.
activities.rationale: The paired setup discriminates between a reactivity-based model and strength/weight/'always reacts' models, because only the correct model predicts exactly one reaction and its direction. Predict-before-observe surfaces the learner's reasoning rather than letting the observation do the work. This mirrors the diagnostic assessment design for the topic.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use the reactivity series to predict the outcome of displacement reactions and study reactions of metals with acids.
Analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-2] they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred.
learnerActions: Before anything is mixed, look at two setups: a strip of magnesium going into blue copper sulfate, and a strip of copper going into colourless magnesium sulfate. Predict which one reacts and WHY.
Commit your reasoning in writing before observing — this prediction is the point of the task.
Observe: only the magnesium-in-copper-sulfate reacts (blue fades, copper deposits on the strip); copper in magnesium sulfate does nothing.
Explain the result using reactivity order, then extend: if magnesium displaces zinc and zinc displaces iron, predict what magnesium does to iron sulfate and how confident you are.
Answer the challenge: why won't ranking metals by how heavy they are predict displacement?
activities.intendedInsight: Ordering metals by reactivity predicts exactly one reaction and names its direction. A model based on 'stronger/heavier/tougher wins' or 'any two metals react' mispredicts. The reasoning, not just the observation, shows understanding.

activities.title: Reactivity ladder reference with history cards
feedback: If a learner leans on the ladder to answer prediction questions without reasoning, prompt them to justify from the relative positions rather than reading off a memorised rank.
Encourage cross-checking: 'Does the reaction you observed match where this metal sits on the ladder?'
activities.rationale: A static annotated ladder is a useful consolidation and reference aid for vocabulary, extraction methods, and the historical strand. Its limit: it does not let a learner generate the order from evidence or test predictions, which is where conceptual understanding forms, so it supports rather than replaces the investigative activities.
learnerActions: Consult a labelled vertical reactivity ladder from potassium (top) to gold (bottom), with carbon and hydrogen marked as reference points, to check vocabulary and ordering.
For a chosen metal, review its reaction with water and acid, its extraction method, and a short history note (gold found native, iron smelted, aluminium electrolytic).
Use the ladder as a lookup aid while doing the prediction and extraction tasks — not as the primary way to first learn the order.
activities.intendedInsight: A reference ladder consolidates vocabulary and the agreed order and links each position to extraction method and history.

constraints: Keep representation at word-equation level and reason qualitatively; defer electrode half-equations and quantitative electrolysis to later (KS4) study.
Build the series from observed evidence (vigour with water and acid) rather than issuing the order as a mnemonic to memorise.

Reactions of the most reactive metals (potassium, sodium) with water must be simulation or teacher demonstration only; learners never handle alkali metals. Limit hands-on pupil work to safer metals (e.g. magnesium, zinc, iron, copper).
Heating metal oxides with carbon is a high-temperature teacher demonstration or simulation, not an open pupil-run task.

The annotated reference ladder is a consolidation and lookup scaffold; on its own it does not let learners derive the order from evidence or test displacement predictions, so pair it with investigative tasks.

Recognition and lookup tasks (reading a ladder, selecting an answer) check ordering and vocabulary but do not elicit independent prediction and explanation; include tasks where the learner states a prediction and its reason before observing.

Use real hands-on displacement work (e.g. an iron nail in copper sulfate) where safe and feasible; a simulated bench is a complement, not a required substitute, and claims about any particular medium being uniquely necessary are not established here.

The historical timeline (native gold, carbon-smelted iron, electrolytic aluminium) is enrichment that illustrates the series; present reactivity as the cause of extraction difficulty, not the reverse.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the teaching principle, not the efficacy of any specific activity.

Two of the three sources (NGSS MS-PS1-2 and the RSC extraction resource) were marked unverified in the source row; the carbon-extraction limit and the NGSS data-interpretation framing are carried over on that basis and should be re-checked.

Safety: Activity 1 keeps the most reactive metals (potassium, sodium) to simulation/teacher demonstration only, with hands-on learner work restricted to safer metals; Activity 3's carbon reduction is likewise demonstration/simulation only because of the high temperatures involved. Matching constraints are included.

Attribution correction this pass: Activity 3's sourceClaims was reduced to the RSC carbon-extraction claim only; the DfE displacement/acids claim was removed there because it supports the topic generally but not the specific carbon-reduction principle of that activity.

Self-audit: the displacement direction logic (more reactive displaces less reactive; reverse does nothing) and the transitive chain (magnesium > zinc > copper ⇒ magnesium displaces copper) are internally consistent and were retained. The reversed cause–effect error about gold (rarity causing low reactivity) was corrected in the activity, not merely caveated.

Self-audit: the claim that carbon reduces oxides below it but not above it is a standard qualitative teaching model, presented qualitatively; aluminium-requires-electrolysis is kept at that level without asserting mechanism beyond KS3 scope. Zinc, lying below carbon, can be carbon-reduced — left to the general principle rather than enumerated.

Original source material framed a dialogue/conversation format and a 3D environment as adding 'nothing' or being unable to substitute; these universal-necessity claims were dropped and replaced with scoped notes on affordances and limits.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: show the two beakers (magnesium in copper sulfate; copper in magnesium sulfate). Ask the child to predict which changes and WHY before dropping the metals in. A 'toughest wins' or 'both react' model mispredicts. Only the magnesium beaker reacts (blue fades, copper deposits). The pre-observation reasoning by reactivity order is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Why can carbon extract iron from iron oxide but NOT aluminium from aluminium oxide?
Gold is found as pure nuggets in rivers but iron is always in rocks as ore — what does that tell you about their reactivity?
If zinc displaces copper, and magnesium displaces zinc, what does magnesium do to copper sulfate — and how sure are you?
Someone ranks metals by how heavy they are. Why won't that predict displacement?
assess.correctAnswer: Only magnesium-in-copper-sulfate reacts: magnesium is MORE reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from the solution (blue fades, copper coats the strip). Copper-in-magnesium-sulfate does nothing because copper is LESS reactive than magnesium and can't displace it. The rule: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its compound. Full marks turn on ordering by reactivity, not on which looks stronger/heavier.

errorPatterns.pattern: reactivity means how hard/strong/heavy or how dangerous a metal is ('copper is tougher so it wins')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate chemical reactivity from physical strength — soft, light sodium is far MORE reactive than hard, dense gold. Rank by how eagerly each reacts, not by hardness.
errorPatterns.distractor: Copper reacts, because copper is a tougher, stronger metal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts the reaction by physical toughness or density rather than position in the reactivity series

errorPatterns.pattern: any two metals will react if you put them together ('metals always react with each other')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Displacement only runs one way — more reactive displaces less reactive; the reverse does nothing. Line up several pairs and predict each using the series.
errorPatterns.distractor: Both react, because whenever you mix two metals something happens.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts both mixtures react, with no notion of direction

errorPatterns.pattern: gold is unreactive because it is rare/precious (cause and effect reversed)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Flip it: gold is found as pure nuggets and never tarnishes BECAUSE it's unreactive; iron must be smelted and aluminium needs electrolysis because they're more reactive. Reactivity explains extraction history.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: explains gold's low reactivity by its rarity/value rather than the other way round

responseLevels.gap: Predicts by strength/weight/rarity or says any two metals react; can't name which of the pair reacts or why.
responseLevels.full: Orders metals by reactivity, predicts displacement direction for any pair, explains extraction method by position (native gold, carbon-smelted iron, electrolysed aluminium), and reasons that reactivity CAUSES the extraction difficulty — not the reverse.
responseLevels.partial: Predicts the magnesium case correctly and cites 'more reactive displaces less reactive', but can't extend to extraction (carbon/aluminium) or chain multiple displacements — the rule without its reach.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I drop a strip of magnesium into blue copper sulfate solution, and separately a strip of copper into colourless magnesium sulfate solution. In ONE of them a reaction happens and in the other nothing does. Which one reacts — and the important part, WHY that one and not the other?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The paired setup is the discriminator: a child who orders metals by reactivity predicts exactly one reaction and names the direction; a child who thinks 'the stronger/harder/heavier metal wins' or that any two metals react cannot say which, or predicts both. The reason, not the observation, reveals the model.
